read.sections.0.heading.source: Sources are clues about the past
read.sections.0.heading.back: Sources are clues about the past

read.sections.0.text.note: "Nguồn" for source, as in KEY_TERMS (alternative: "tư liệu"). "Manh mối trong một câu đố" for "clue in a puzzle". Is "nhà sử học" plus "nghiên cứu quá khứ" natural for a 12-year-old? Please check.
read.sections.0.text.source: Nobody alive today saw the world as it was 1,000 years ago, so how do we know about it? A historian is a person who studies the past by looking for sources. A source is anything that gives us information about the past. Letters, photographs, drawings, tools, receipts, buildings and maps can all be sources, and so can memories that older people share. Each source is like a clue in a puzzle. The Riverstone drawing, receipt and diary are three sources about one market. A historian uses clues like these as evidence and then makes a claim about what happened.
read.sections.0.text.back: No one alive today has seen the world as it was 1,000 years ago. So how do we know about that world? A historian is a person who studies the past by looking for sources. A source is anything that gives us information about the past. Letters, photographs, drawings, tools, receipts, buildings and maps can all be sources, and so can the things older people remember and tell. Each source is like a clue in a puzzle. The drawing, receipt and diary in Riverstone are three sources about the same market. Historians use clues like these as evidence, then make a claim about what happened.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: Very short sentences; "nhận định" for claim is a slightly abstract word for the simpler level but is a glossary word and must stay.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: Nobody today saw the world long ago. So how do we learn about it? A historian is a person who studies the past. Historians look at sources. A source tells us something about the past. It can be a letter, a photo or a tool. It can be a story that an older person tells. Each source is a clue. We use clues as evidence. Evidence helps us make a claim about the past.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: No one today has seen the world of long ago. So how do we know about it? A historian is a person who studies the past. A historian looks at sources. A source tells us something about the past. A source can be a letter, a photo or a tool. A source can also be a story an older person tells. Each source is a clue. We use clues as evidence. Evidence helps us make a claim about the past.

read.sections.1.text.note: "Nguồn này cho mình biết điều gì": the historian's question is written with "mình" (as the reader asking). Check this sounds natural rather than "chúng ta" or "tôi".
read.sections.1.text.source: Different sources can answer different questions about the past. The receipt shows what one shop sold and the price of each item, so it tells us that rice cost 12 tokens. The drawing shows what the market looked like, with stalls, baskets and a cart. However, the artist may have left some details out. The diary describes what one young person saw and did on market day. It says that traders arrived by boat before sunrise, but one person cannot see everything. So a historian always asks two questions: What does this source tell me, and what can it not tell me?
read.sections.1.text.back: Different sources can answer different questions about the past. A receipt says what a shop sold and the price of each item, so it tells us rice cost 12 tokens. The drawing shows what the market looked like, with stalls, baskets and a pull cart. However, the person who drew it may have left out some details. The diary tells what a young person saw and did on market day. It says the merchants came by boat before sunrise, but one person cannot see everything. So a historian always asks two questions: What does this source tell me, and what does it not tell me?

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Each source answers different questions. The receipt shows prices. Rice cost 12 tokens. The drawing shows what the market looked like. But the artist may leave things out. The diary tells what one young person saw. It says traders came by boat. But one person cannot see everything. So ask two questions. What does this source tell me? What does it not tell me?
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Each source answers different questions. A receipt tells prices. Rice cost 12 tokens. The drawing shows what the market looked like. But the person who drew may have left out some things. The diary tells what a young person saw. The diary says the merchants came by boat. But one person cannot see everything. So ask two questions. What does this source tell me? What does it not tell me?

read.sections.2.text.note: "Bỏ ngỏ" (stay open) for an unanswered question; "nhận định vững" for "strong claim". Check both are natural.
read.sections.2.text.source: One source almost never tells the whole story, so historians compare sources. To compare means to look at two things and notice how they are similar or different. The drawing shows a river, and the diary says that traders came by boat. Together, these clues suggest that the river helped people bring goods to the market. A historian also asks who made each source, and why they made it. Some questions stay open, because none of the sources tells us how many people lived in Riverstone. A strong claim explains what the evidence shows and what we still do not know.
read.sections.2.text.back: One source almost never tells the whole story, so historians compare sources with each other. To compare means to look at two things and notice where they are the same or different. The drawing has a river, and the diary says the merchants came by boat. Together these two clues suggest that the river helped people bring goods to the market. Historians also ask who made each source and why they made it. Some questions stay open, because no source tells us how many people lived in Riverstone. A strong claim explains what the evidence shows and what we still do not know.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: One source does not tell the whole story. So historians compare sources. They look for what is the same and what is different. The drawing shows a river. The diary talks about boats. So the river may have helped traders get to the market. Some things we still do not know. No source says how many people lived there. A good claim says what we know. It also says what we do not know.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: One source does not tell the whole story. So historians compare sources. They look for what is the same and what is different. The drawing has a river. The diary talks about boats. So the river may have helped the merchants get to the market. There are things we still do not know. No source says how many people lived there. A good claim says what we know. It also says what we do not know.

write.example.note: The example answer is in the first person ("Mình nghĩ ..."), as the starters are. Check it is natural for a learner's own writing.
write.example.source: I think Riverstone Market was a busy place where people traded food. The drawing shows stalls selling food and cloth. It also shows people carrying baskets. The diary also shows that the market was crowded. It says traders came by boat before sunrise. Together, these sources suggest that the river helped traders bring goods to the market. But the sources do not tell us how many people lived in Riverstone. They also do not tell us what the market was like on other days.
write.example.back: I think Riverstone market used to be a lively place where people bought and sold food. The drawing shows stalls selling food and cloth. It also shows people carrying baskets. The diary also shows the market was very crowded. The diary says the merchants came by boat before the sun rose. Put together, these sources suggest that the river helped the merchants bring goods to the market. But the sources do not tell us how many people lived in Riverstone. They also do not tell how the market was on other days.

watch.summary.note: "Nguồn trực tiếp" for "primary source". The usual school term is "tư liệu gốc" or "nguồn sử liệu gốc", but "nguồn gốc" would be confused with "origin". "Nguồn trực tiếp" is easier for a young reader. Please choose the term; it recurs in watch.why and watch.keyPoints here and in Lesson 2. | Review: Original could be read as 'at the moment you are learning'; English means the period being studied. Also: 'nguồn trực tiếp' for 'primary source' is a calque (not in KEY_TERMS); a native speaker should choose between nguồn trực tiếp / tư liệu gốc / nguồn gốc. [Reviewer changed: được tạo ra vào thời điểm bạn đang tìm hiểu → được tạo ra vào đúng thời kì mà bạn đang tìm hiểu]
watch.summary.source: This short video explains primary sources. A primary source was made at the time you are studying, often by someone who was there. Letters, diaries, photos, receipts, maps and tools can all be primary sources. They do not have to be famous or special. An everyday receipt can show what people bought and what it cost. A diary can show what one person saw and felt. But each primary source shows only part of the story. So historians ask who made it, when, and why. Then they compare it with other sources. In this lesson, the drawing, the receipt and the diary are all primary sources. Together, they tell us more than any one of them alone.
watch.summary.back: This short video explains primary sources. A primary source is made at the time you are learning about, often by a person who was there. Letters, diaries, photos, receipts, maps and tools can all be primary sources. They do not need to be famous or special. An ordinary receipt can show what people bought and how much it cost. A diary can show what a person saw and felt. But each primary source shows only part of the story. So historians ask who made it, when and why. Then they compare it with other sources. In this lesson, the drawing, receipt and diary are all primary sources. Put together, they tell us more than any one source standing alone.
